title: On the phone, and doing things right now
goal: Make phone calls in Korean — the hardest situation for beginners, with no face to read — and add the "-ing" form -고 있어요, which hasn't appeared until now.
bekal: opening and closing a phone call correctly
using -고 있어요 for actions in progress
asking to speak to someone else
leaving a message and promising to call back
understanding the set phrases Koreans use on the phone

dialogs.title: 대화 — Calling a friend
dialogs.intro: Ani calls Suji. Notice that opening and closing a call in Korea consists almost entirely of set phrases you can learn as they are.

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.literal: hello, Suji — Ms.? I — Ani — am.

lines.speaker: 수지:
lines.id: Oh, Ani! What are you doing right now?
lines.literal: ah, Ani — Ms.! now — what — doing — are?

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: I'm studying at the library. And you?
lines.literal: library-at — studying — am. Suji — Ms. — as-for — polite?

lines.speaker: 수지:
lines.literal: I — as-for — now — rice — eating — am. what — matter — exists?

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: Do you remember our plans tomorrow? We agreed to meet at one.
lines.literal: tomorrow — appointment — remembering — are? one — o'clock-at — meet-to — decided.

lines.speaker: 수지:
lines.id: Oh, right! I almost forgot. Thanks!

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: By any chance, could we change the time? How about two?
lines.literal: by-any-chance — time — change-will — possibility — exists? two — o'clock — as-for — how?

lines.speaker: 수지:
lines.id: Yes, that's fine. But my friend is waiting for me right now.
lines.literal: yes, fine. by-the-way, now — friend — subject — waiting — is.

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: Oh, sorry. I'll call you back later.

lines.speaker: 수지:
lines.id: No problem. See you tomorrow at two, then!
lines.literal: it-isn't. then, tomorrow — two — o'clock-at — see!

notes: **여보세요 is used only on the phone.** It isn't an ordinary "hello" — saying it to someone standing in front of you sounds funny. It comes from "look here", and both the caller and the person answering use it.

**들어가세요 as a phone goodbye means "go in", and yes, that's odd.** It's a leftover from the days of public phones outside the home, when ending a call meant sending the other person home. Today it's simply the standard closing, fully polite and very common.
**-고 있어요 expresses an action in progress.** 공부해요 = I study (a habit, or in general). 공부하**고 있어요** = I'm studying (right now, at this moment). Like English "I study" versus "I'm studying".

**⚠️ -고 있어요 is used far less often than learners expect.** For most things happening now, the plain 해요 form is enough and more natural — English speakers tend to overuse -고 있어요 because English needs "-ing" for anything in progress. Use it only when you really want to stress "right at this moment", as in the phone question 지금 뭐 하고 있어요?

**약속 means an appointment to meet, not just a promise.** 약속이 있어요 = "I have plans" is a complete excuse that needs no further explanation — just like 일이 있어요. Asking who the plans are with is considered a bit pushy.

**-기로 했어요 means "agreed to" or "decided to".** 만나기로 했어요 = we agreed to meet. It turns the verb into a noun with -기, then "decides on it" with 로 하다. For now learn it whole; it comes up often in talk about shared plans.
**혹시 means "by any chance" or "perhaps", and it softens any question.** 혹시 시간 있어요? sounds far more polite than 시간 있어요?, because it leaves room for the other person to say no. It works exactly like 좀.
**까먹다 is casual for "to forget"** — literally "to peel and eat". The neutral form is 잊어버리다. The pattern -(으)ㄹ 뻔했어요 ("almost") is also worth knowing: 늦을 뻔했어요 = I was almost late.

grammars.title: -고 있어요 — be doing
body: Attach **-고 있어요** straight to the stem. No choice of forms, just like -고 싶어요 and -고.
after: **The honorific form changes 있다 to 계시다:** 뭐 하고 **계세요**? = "What are you doing?" (respectfully). A direct application of the honorific verbs in unit 8.
⚠️ **Adjectives can't take -고 있어요.** 예쁘고 있어요 is not a sentence. Adjectives describe a state that already holds, so the plain 해요 form is enough: 예뻐요.
**Some verbs change meaning with -고 있어요:** 입고 있어요 means "is wearing" (a state), not "is putting on clothes" (an action). Same for 알고 있어요 ("know") and 기억하고 있어요 ("remember").

grammars.title: Set phrases for the phone
body: Phoning is the hardest situation for beginners because there are no faces or gestures to help. Luckily, almost every opening and closing is a fixed phrase.

head: Situation
Phrase
Meaning
rows: Could I speak to Minjun, please?

after: **잘 안 들려요 is a lifesaver.** It's honest, polite, and instantly makes the other person slow down and speak more clearly — far more useful than pretending to understand.
**For official matters, Koreans prefer calling to texting**, including booking a table and asking about opening hours. You'll use some of the phrases above more than you'd expect.

blocks.text: Most written conversation in Korea happens on KakaoTalk, and the language is far shorter than speech. Knowing the abbreviations stops the messages you receive from looking like code.
⚠️ These abbreviations are **only** for friends your age and younger. Sending ㅇㅇ to your boss or teacher is as rude as replying "k" to a professor.

head: Sentence
Meaning
rows: If it's convenient, could we talk on the phone now?
Thank you. Have a nice day.

blocks.title: 좋은 하루 되세요
items: The safest and most common way to end a message — the equivalent of "have a nice day". Safe with anyone, including your boss.
For the evening and night: 좋은 저녁 되세요, 좋은 밤 되세요. For the weekend: 좋은 주말 보내세요.
To reply, 네, 감사합니다 is enough — or just send the same phrase back.
